He said: It was reported to me that the polytheists would say to the Muslims who had entered the Fire: "What did what you used to worship avail you?" He said: Then God will become angry for them, and He will say to the angels and the prophets: "Intercede!" They will intercede, and they will come out of the Fire, until Iblis stretches himself up hoping that he will come out with them. He said: At that point, ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Hajjaj narrated to us, he said: Hammad narrated to us, from Ibrahim, that he said regarding the saying of God, mighty and majestic, ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾: He said: Those in the Fire among the polytheists will say to the Muslims: "What did 'There is no god but God' avail you?" He said: Then God will become angry for them, and He will say: "Whoever was a Muslim, let him come out of the Fire." He said: At that point ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, regarding His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾. He said: The people of the Fire will say: "We were people of polytheism and disbelief. What is the matter with these monotheists? What did their worship of Him avail them?" He said: Then whoever among the Muslims was in the Fire will come out. He said: At that point ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: al-Thawri informed us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from Khusayf, from Mujahid, who said: The people of the Fire will say to the monotheists: "What did your faith avail you?" He said: When they say that, [God] will say: "Bring out whoever has in his heart the weight of an atom." At that point ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Muslim narrated to us, he said: Hisham narrated to us, from Hammad, who said: I asked Ibrahim about the saying of God, mighty and majestic, ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾. He said: The disbelievers reproach the people of monotheism: "What did 'There is no god but God' avail you?" Then God will become angry for them, and will command the prophets and the angels, and they will intercede, and the people of monotheism will come out, until Iblis stretches himself up hoping to come out. That is His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Ahmad narrated to us, he said: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Salam narrated to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid, who said: This is concerning the people of Hell, when they see them coming out of the Fire: ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, he said: Hammad narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Mujahid, who said: When God has finished judging between His creatures, He says: "Whoever was a Muslim, let him enter Paradise." At that point ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us; and al-Hasan narrated to me, he said: Shababah narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, he said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding his saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾: He said: It is the Day of Resurrection.

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn 'Ata' narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾: He said: In it there are two aspects. Some say: When the disbeliever is present at death, he wishes he had been a Muslim. Others say: Rather, God punishes some people of monotheism in the Fire for their sins, and the polytheists recognize them and say: "What did your worship of your Lord avail you, since He has cast you into the Fire?" Then He will become angry for them and bring them out, and He says ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

* Ibn Waki' narrated to us, he said: my father narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾: He said: It was revealed concerning those who will come out of the Fire.

* Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾: And that, by God, is on the Day of Resurrection, when they wish they had been Muslims in the world.

* Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾. [Meaning: like the narration of Bishr before him, because both chains of narration end with Qatadah.]

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Ata', from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: God will not cease to admit [people] to Paradise and intercede until He says: "Whoever was among the Muslims, let him enter Paradise." At that point He says ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 15, verse 3–5:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; but they will come to know.﴾ (3)

His exalted mention says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Leave them, O Muhammad, these polytheists, to eat in this world what they are going to eat, and to enjoy its pleasures and their desires in it until their term, which I have set for them, and let hope distract them from taking their share of obedience to God in it, and from providing for their return (to Him) from it with what brings them near to their Lord. They will come to know tomorrow, when they arrive before Him. They will have perished in their disbelief in God and their polytheism when they witness the punishment of God, that they were, in their enjoyment of the pleasures and desires they used to enjoy in it, in loss and ruin.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And We did not destroy any city but that it had a known decree.﴾ (4)

His exalted mention says: ﴿And We did not destroy﴾ O Muhammad ﴿any﴾ people ﴿city﴾ of the cities whose people We destroyed in the past ﴿but that it had a known decree﴾. He says: but that it had a fixed term and a known period. We do not destroy them until they reach it, and when they reach it, We destroy them at that time. So He says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): likewise the people of your city, from which you come, which is Makkah, We do not destroy its polytheist inhabitants except after their decree reaches its term, because it is part of My decree that I do not destroy the people of any city except after their decree reaches its term.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay it.﴾ (5)

His exalted mention says: No nation's destruction precedes the term that God has set as its term for destruction, nor is its destruction delayed beyond the term that has been set for it.

As related:

Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, regarding His saying ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay it﴾, he said: We hold that when its term arrives, it is not delayed an hour nor advanced. As for what has not yet reached its term, God delays what He wills and advances what He wills.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly a madman. Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful?"﴾ (15:6–7)**

Allah, exalted is His remembrance, says: The polytheists from your own people, O Muhammad, said, ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an, in which Allah mentioned the admonitions for His creation. ﴿You are truly a madman﴾ for your calling us to follow you and to abandon our gods. ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels﴾. They said: Why do you not bring us the angels as witnesses to the truth of what you say? ﴿If you are of the truthful﴾, meaning: if you are truthful that Allah, exalted is He, has sent you to us as a messenger and sent down to you a Book, then the Lord who did what you describe is not incapable of sending an angel from among His angels with you, as a proof for you against us, a sign of your prophethood, and a confirmation of your message.

The Arabs use *lawma* in place of *lula* (why/if not), and *lula* in place of *lawma*. Of this is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

*"Lawma al-ḥayā'u wa lawma al-dīn 'ibtukumā*
*bi-ba'ḍi mā fīkumā idh 'ibtumā 'awaray"*

[The verse is by Ibn Muqbil, from an ode whose opening verses are in al-Hamasa (d: 113). It is evidence that *lawma* is used with the meaning of *lula* (expressing the non-occurrence of one thing due to the presence of another). In the verse, it carries the meaning of *tahḍīḍ* (urging). Abu 'Ubayda said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an: "*Lawma* and *lula* have the same function." He cited Ibn Muqbil's verse, and the author (al-Tabari) took it from him.]

That is, "If not for shame and if not for religion, I would have reproached you both for some of what is in you, when you two reproached me for my defect."

He means: "If not for shame."

The people of ta'wil (interpretation, exegesis) have said what is similar to what we have said regarding the meaning of *al-dhikr* (the Reminder).

Those who said that:

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, regarding ﴿the Reminder has been sent down﴾, he said: "The Qur'an."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 15, verse 8:

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be reprieved﴾ (8).

The reciters differed over the reading of His saying ﴿We do not send down the angels﴾. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra read ﴿Not do the angels come down﴾ with a ta' (tanazzilu) and with a fatha on it, and with the raising of "the angels" (al-malaikatu), meaning: the angels do not come down, the verb being attributed to the angels. The majority of the reciters of Kufa read ﴿We do not send down the angels﴾ with a nun on tunazzilu and a shadda on the zay, and with the accusative on "the angels" (al-malaikata), meaning: We do not send them down, and "the angels" is then in the accusative as the object of the verb "send down." Some of the reciters of Kufa read it ﴿Not are the angels sent down﴾ with the raising of "the angels" and with a ta' and damma on tunazzilu, in the passive form (ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu, the verb whose subject is not named).

Abu Ja'far said: All three readings are close in meaning, because when God sends down the angels to one of His messengers, they descend to him, and when they descend to him, they descend by God's sending them down to him. Whichever of these three readings a reciter uses, he is correct. However, I prefer that the reader not go beyond one of the two readings mentioned from the people of Medina, or the other one held by the majority of the Kufan reciters, because that is the well-known reading among the common people. As for the other, namely the reading of those who read ﴿Not are sent down﴾ with a damma on the ta' of tunazzilu and the raising of "the angels," it is an irregular (shadhdh) reading, and few have recited it.

So the meaning of the statement is: We do not send down Our angels except with truth, meaning with the message to Our messengers, or with punishment for whoever We intend to punish. And if We were to send down to these polytheists, in response to what they ask of you, a sign, and they disbelieved, they would not be reprieved and delayed in punishment; rather, they would be hastened to it, as We did with the nations before them, who asked for signs and then disbelieved when the signs came to them, so We hastened them with punishment.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said regarding His saying ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, he said: Abu Asim related to us, he said: Isa related to us. And al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us. And al-Hasan ibn Muhammad related to us, he said: Shababa related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us. And al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, he said: Shibl related to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾, he said: "With the message and the punishment."

- al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.

The commentary on the words of His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ (15:9).

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿and indeed We will be its guardian﴾. He said: "And indeed We are its guardians against anything false being added to it that is not part of it, or anything that is part of it being diminished, namely its rulings, its limits and its obligations." The pronoun in His saying ﴿its﴾ refers back to "the Reminder."

Along the lines of what we have said, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have also said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us. And al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us. And al-Hasan related to me, saying: Shababa related to us, saying: Warqa related to us. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿and indeed We will be its guardian﴾, he said: "With Us."

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder and indeed We will be its guardian﴾. He said, in another verse, ﴿falsehood cannot approach it﴾ [41:42], and falsehood is Iblis, ﴿from before it or behind it﴾ [41:42]. So Allah sent it down, then guarded it, and Iblis cannot add any falsehood to it or diminish any truth from it. Allah preserved it from that.

- Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, ﴿and indeed We will be its guardian﴾, he said: "Allah preserved it from Satan adding any falsehood to it or diminishing any truth from it."

It has also been said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: "And indeed We will be guardians of Muhammad against whoever among his enemies intends him harm."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 15, verses 10–13:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We sent [messengers] before you among the sects of the former peoples (10). And there never came to them a messenger except that they used to mock him (11).﴾

He, exalted is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Indeed We sent, O Muhammad, before you messengers among the former nations. The mention of the messengers is omitted, being sufficiently indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed We sent before you﴾. By "shiya' al-awwalin" (sects of the former peoples) He means the nations of the former peoples; its singular is shi'ah, and the word is also used for a man's supporters: his shi'ah.

This is also what the people of interpretation have said.

Those who said this:

- Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: 'Abd Allah related to us, he said: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Indeed We sent [messengers] before you among the sects of the former peoples﴾ means: the nations of the former peoples.

- Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Ishaq informed us, he said: Hisham related to us, from 'Amr, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed We sent [messengers] before you among the sects of the former peoples﴾, he said: among the nations.

* *

And His saying ﴿And there never came to them a messenger except that they used to mock him﴾

He says: And there never came to the sects of the former peoples a messenger from Allah whom He sent to them calling them to His monotheism and to submission to obedience to Him, except that they used to mock him: meaning, except that they used to ridicule the messenger whom Allah sent to them, out of insolence and rebellion against their Lord.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals (12). They do not believe in it, and the example of the former peoples has already passed (13).﴾

He, exalted is He, says: Just as We caused disbelief to enter into the hearts of the sects of the former peoples through mocking the messengers, so We do likewise to the hearts of the polytheists of your people who have committed crime by disbelieving in Allah. ﴿They do not believe in it﴾: meaning, they do not affirm the Reminder that has been sent down to you. The pronoun in His saying ﴿We let it enter﴾ refers to the mocking of the messengers and denying them.

As follows:

- Al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾, he said: the denial.

- Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals. They do not believe in it﴾, he said: when they denied, Allah caused into their hearts that they should not believe in it.

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: al-Thawri informed us, from Humayd, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾, he said: the polytheism.

- al-Muthanna related to me, he said: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal related to us, he said: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us, from Humayd, who said: I recited the whole Qur'an to al-Hasan in the house of Abu Khalifah, and he explained it all in affirmative terms. So I asked him about His saying ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾, and he said: deeds they will do which they had not done.

- al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Suwayd related to us, he said: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Humayd al-Tawil, who said: I recited the whole Qur'an to al-Hasan, and he explained it only in affirmative terms. He said: I stopped at "nasluk-hu" and he said: the polytheism. Ibn al-Mubarak said: I heard Sufyan on His saying ﴿nasluk-hu﴾, he said: we make it [enter].

- Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals. They do not believe in it﴾, he said: they are as Allah said; He is the one who misguided them and withheld faith from them. The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 15, verses 14–15:

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about who is meant by His words ﴿فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾ ("and they continued to ascend through it"). Some of them said: the meaning of the speech is: "Had We opened for these people who say to you, O Muhammad, ﴿لَوْ مَا تَأْتِينَا بِالْمَلائِكَةِ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ﴾ ('Why do not the angels come to us, if you are among the truthful?'), a gate from the sky, and the angels were ascending through it while they saw them plainly, ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَسْحُورُونَ﴾ ('they would surely say: 'Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people under sorcery.'")

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, he said: my father told me, he said: my paternal uncle told me, he said: my father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿وَلَوْ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾, he said: "Had We opened for them a gate from the sky, and the angels were ascending through it, the people of polytheism would say: 'It has only taken hold of our sight, confused us, and bewitched us.' That is their saying: ﴿لَوْ مَا تَأْتِينَا بِالْمَلائِكَةِ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ﴾."

• Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾: "The angels would continue to ascend through it, the children of Adam seeing them plainly, ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَسْحُورُونَ﴾."

• Al-Qasim told us, he said: al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His words ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِي نزلَ عَلَيْهِ الذِّكْرُ إِنَّكَ لَمَجْنُونٌ لَوْ مَا تَأْتِينَا بِالْمَلائِكَةِ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ﴾ ("O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, indeed you are mad! Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are among the truthful?"), he said: "What lies between that and His words ﴿وَلَوْ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾ returns to His words ﴿لَوْ مَا تَأْتِينَا بِالْمَلائِكَةِ﴾, and what lies between them." Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The angels were ascending, so they looked at them." ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾ — he said: "Quraysh say it."

• Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la told us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿وَلَوْ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾, he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had God opened for them a gate from the sky, and the angels were ascending through it — meaning they would be going back and forth through it, coming and going — ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾."

• I was told, from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman told us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His words (﴿وَلَوْ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾), meaning the angels: "He says: 'Had I opened for the polytheists a gate from the sky, and they looked at the angels ascending between the sky and the earth, the polytheists would say: ﴿نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَسْحُورُونَ﴾ — we have been bewitched, and this is not the truth.' Do you not see that they said before this verse: ﴿لَوْ مَا تَأْتِينَا بِالْمَلائِكَةِ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ﴾?"

• Al-Muthanna told me, he said: Ishaq told us, he said: Hisham told us, from 'Umar, from Nasr, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿وَلَوْ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾, he said: "Had I opened a gate from the sky through which the angels ascended between the sky and the earth, the polytheists would say ﴿بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَسْحُورُونَ﴾. Do you not see that they said ﴿لَوْ مَا تَأْتِينَا بِالْمَلائِكَةِ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ﴾?"

Others said: It refers only to the children of Adam.

The meaning of the speech according to them is: "Had We opened for these polytheists from your people, O Muhammad, a gate from the sky, and they themselves were ascending through it, ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾."

Mention of those who said this:

• Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿وَلَوْ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَظَلُّوا فِيهِ يَعْرُجُونَ﴾, Qatadah said: "al-Hasan used to say: 'Had this been done to the children of Adam, and they were ascending through it' — meaning they would be going back and forth — ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَسْحُورُونَ﴾."

As for His words ﴿يَعْرُجُونَ﴾, its meaning is: they climb up through it and ascend. It is said from it: "'araja (ya'ruju) 'urujan" when one climbs and ascends. The singular of al-ma'arij is mu'arrij and mi'raj. From this is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"To a noble ancestry, which raised the man before him,
whose father has in it ladders (ma'arij) of a stairway."

[[I did not find the verse in the Diwan of Kuthayyir printed in Algeria. Al-hasab: established honour in forefathers; al-'awd: ancient; banā (with alif): built, because it is the building of honour and glory; al-ma'arij: plural of mu'arrij (with kasra or fatha on the mim), which is that by which one ascends, i.e., climbs.]]

It has been related that "'ariga ya'rigu" with a kasra on the ra' in the imperfect.

* *

As for His words ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾:

He says: "These polytheists whose description He, may His praise be exalted, has mentioned would say: 'This is not the truth; our eyes have only been dazzled.'"

The readers (qurra') differed regarding the recitation of His word ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾. The people of Madina and Iraq read ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ with the kaf shaddah (doubled), meaning: "covered and veiled." So Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used to say, as has been related to me from him. It is related from Mujahid that he used to recite ﴿لَقالُوا إنَّمَا سُكِرَتْ﴾ (without doubling).

• Al-Harith told me of this, he said: al-Qasim told us, he said: I heard al-Kisa'i narrate from Hamzah, from Shibl, from Mujahid, that he recited it ﴿سُكِرَتْ أَبْصارُنا﴾ lightly (without doubling). Mujahid, in his recitation of that, took its meaning to be: "our eyes have been prevented from seeing and looking, from the sukur of the wind, which is its stillness and calm. It is said from it: 'the wind sakarat' when it becomes still and calm." It has been related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that he used to say: "It is derived from the intoxication of drink (sukr al-sharab), and its meaning is: intoxication has veiled our eyes."

As for the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil), they differed about its interpretation. Some of them said: the meaning of ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ is: "were blocked up."

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, he said: Abu 'Asim told us, he said: Warqa' told us; and al-Hasan ibn Muhammad told us, he said: Shababah told us, he said: Warqa' told us; and al-Muthanna told me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah told us, he said: Shibl told us; and al-Muthanna told me, he said: Ishaq told us, he said: 'Abd Allah told us, all from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾, he said: "It means: were blocked up."

• Al-Qasim told us, he said: al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, similarly.

• Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad told us, he said: Hajjaj, meaning Ibn Muhammad, told us, from Ibn Jurayj, he said: Ibn Kathir told me, he said: "It blocked up."

• I was told, from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd told us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His words ﴿سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾: "It means: blocked up."

So it seems that Mujahid, in his saying and his interpretation of it as "blocked up," meant that it means "prevented from looking," just as water is "sukkira" (dammed) when it is prevented from flowing by being held in a place with the dam (sikr) by which it is dammed.

Others said: the meaning of "sukkirat" is: "were taken" (ukhidhat).

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la told us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾, he says: "Our eyes were taken."

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, he said: my father told me, he said: my paternal uncle told me, he said: my father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "It has only taken our sight, and confused us, and bewitched us."

• Al-Qasim told us, he said: al-Husayn told us, he said: Abu Sufyan told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾, he says: "Our eyes were bewitched," he says: "Our eyes were taken."

• Al-Muthanna told me, he said: Ishaq told us, he said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad told us, he said: Shaybān told us, from Qatadah, he said: "Whoever reads ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ with doubling means: blocked up, and whoever reads ﴿سُكرَتْ﴾ lightly means: bewitched." It seems these people directed the meaning of His word ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ to: their eyes were bewitched, so what they see is confused for them, and they cannot distinguish between what is true of what they see and other than it. From the saying of the Arabs: "sukkira 'ala fulan ra'yuh" — when his opinion became confused for him regarding what he wanted, so he did not know the right course in it from other than it. When he resolved on an opinion, they said: "the sukkir has left him."

Others said: it is derived from intoxication (al-sukr), and its meaning is: "fainting came over our eyes, so we do not see, as intoxication does to its companion. That is when one is made to spin around and his sight is veiled, like the dizzy one, so he does not see."

Mention of those who said this:

• Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾: "Sukkirat, the drunkard who does not understand."

Others said: the meaning of that is: "were blinded" (ʿumiyat).

Mention of those who said this:

• Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad told us, he said: 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn 'Ata' told us, from al-Kalbi, ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾, he said: "Were blinded."

The most correct of these sayings in my view is the saying of the one who said: the meaning of that is: "our eyes were taken and bewitched, so they do not perceive a thing as it is, and the edge of their sight has gone, and its light has been extinguished, as one says of a hot thing when its boiling has gone and the edge of its heat has calmed: 'sakara yaskuru.'" Al-Muthanna ibn Jandal al-Tuhawi said:

"Winter has come and the qabr has huddled,
and the viper has become sluggish, after it used to appear.
And the eye of the heat-haze (al-harur) began to sukur."

[[These are three verses of Jandal ibn al-Muthanna al-Tuhawi. Ijtha'alla: gathered and contracted. Al-qabr, like al-qanbar: a kind of bird like sparrows; its singular is qabrah and qanbarah. Al-harur: the heat. It is said: "sakarat 'aynuhu yaskuru" when it is bewildered and stilled from looking; "sakara al-harr yaskuru" when the heat calmed and subsided. Abu 'Ubaydah cited these verses in Majaz al-Qur'an (1: 337–338) at His words "sakarat abṣāruna," saying: that is, "covered with dizziness, so its look went away and was extinguished." He said: "The winter has come," etc., and added a verse before the last one, which is: "And the sun rose upon it, a helmet." He explained the last verse, which is the witness, with his saying: "that its heat goes away and subsides." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "sakarat abṣāruna": derived from the intoxication of drink, as if the eye was afflicted by what afflicts the drinker of an intoxicant when he is drunk. Al-Farra' said: its meaning: "was held back and prevented from looking."]]

That is, it calms, goes away, and is extinguished. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Before the splitting of dawn and the al-tahajjur,
and their plunging into the night when it sukur."

[[The verse is in the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah (Cambridge edition, 1919), p. 202, and before it: "They brought you with a company of swift, lean [camels], the eyes of whose [riders] are sunken, whose noble parts (ashraf) have been worn by the tabakkur." Khawṣ: sunken-eyed; ashrafuhā: their humps; al-tabakkur: the travel of the morning; al-tahajjur: the travel of the midday heat; yaskuru: their sight is covered by its darkness. His saying "al-tahajjur" in the nominative is coordinated with "al-tabakkur" in the preceding verse.]]

That is: "when its heat calms." It has been related from Qays that she said: "sakarat al-rih taskuru sukuran," meaning: "it calmed." Even if that is correct from her, the meaning of "sukirat" and "sukkirat," with lightness and doubling, is close; however, the reading that I do not permit anything other than in the Qur'an is ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ with doubling, due to the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it, and it is not permissible to oppose what they have agreed upon.

• Al-Qasim told us, he said: al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, similarly.

• Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad told us, he said: Hajjaj, meaning Ibn Muhammad, told us, from Ibn Jurayj, he said: Ibn Kathir told me, he said: "It blocked up."

• I was told, from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd told us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His words ﴿سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾: "It means: blocked up."

So it seems that Mujahid, in his saying and his interpretation of it as "blocked up," meant that it means "prevented from looking," just as water is "sukkira" (dammed) when it is prevented from flowing by being held in a place with the dam (sikr) by which it is dammed.

Others said: the meaning of "sukkirat" is: "were taken" (ukhidhat).

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la told us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾, he says: "Our eyes were taken."

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, he said: my father told me, he said: my paternal uncle told me, he said: my father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "It has only taken our sight, and confused us, and bewitched us."

• Al-Qasim told us, he said: al-Husayn told us, he said: Abu Sufyan told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿لَقَالُوا إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾, he says: "Our eyes were bewitched," he says: "Our eyes were taken."

• Al-Muthanna told me, he said: Ishaq told us, he said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad told us, he said: Shaybān told us, from Qatadah, he said: "Whoever reads ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ with doubling means: blocked up, and whoever reads ﴿سُكرَتْ﴾ lightly means: bewitched." It seems these people directed the meaning of His word ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ to: their eyes were bewitched, so what they see is confused for them, and they cannot distinguish between what is true of what they see and other than it. From the saying of the Arabs: "sukkira 'ala fulan ra'yuh" — when his opinion became confused for him regarding what he wanted, so he did not know the right course in it from other than it. When he resolved on an opinion, they said: "the sukkir has left him."

Others said: it is derived from intoxication (al-sukr), and its meaning is: "fainting came over our eyes, so we do not see, as intoxication does to its companion. That is when one is made to spin around and his sight is veiled, like the dizzy one, so he does not see."

Mention of those who said this:

• Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا﴾: "Sukkirat, the drunkard who does not understand."

Others said: the meaning of that is: "were blinded" (ʿumiyat).

Mention of those who said this:

• Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad told us, he said: 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn 'Ata' told us, from al-Kalbi, ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾, he said: "Were blinded."

The most correct of these sayings in my view is the saying of the one who said: the meaning of that is: "our eyes were taken and bewitched, so they do not perceive a thing as it is, and the edge of their sight has gone, and its light has been extinguished, as one says of a hot thing when its boiling has gone and the edge of its heat has calmed: 'sakara yaskuru.'" Al-Muthanna ibn Jandal al-Tuhawi said:

"Winter has come and the qabr has huddled,
and the viper has become sluggish, after it used to appear.
And the eye of the heat-haze (al-harur) began to sukur."

[[These are three verses of Jandal ibn al-Muthanna al-Tuhawi. Ijtha'alla: gathered and contracted. Al-qabr, like al-qanbar: a kind of bird like sparrows; its singular is qabrah and qanbarah. Al-harur: the heat. It is said: "sakarat 'aynuhu yaskuru" when it is bewildered and stilled from looking; "sakara al-harr yaskuru" when the heat calmed and subsided. Abu 'Ubaydah cited these verses in Majaz al-Qur'an (1: 337–338) at His words "sakarat abṣāruna," saying: that is, "covered with dizziness, so its look went away and was extinguished." He said: "The winter has come," etc., and added a verse before the last one, which is: "And the sun rose upon it, a helmet." He explained the last verse, which is the witness, with his saying: "that its heat goes away and subsides." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "sakarat abṣāruna": derived from the intoxication of drink, as if the eye was afflicted by what afflicts the drinker of an intoxicant when he is drunk. Al-Farra' said: its meaning: "was held back and prevented from looking."]]

That is, it calms, goes away, and is extinguished. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Before the splitting of dawn and the al-tahajjur,
and their plunging into the night when it sukur."

[[The verse is in the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah (Cambridge edition, 1919), p. 202, and before it: "They brought you with a company of swift, lean [camels], the eyes of whose [riders] are sunken, whose noble parts (ashraf) have been worn by the tabakkur." Khawṣ: sunken-eyed; ashrafuhā: their humps; al-tabakkur: the travel of the morning; al-tahajjur: the travel of the midday heat; yaskuru: their sight is covered by its darkness. His saying "al-tahajjur" in the nominative is coordinated with "al-tabakkur" in the preceding verse.]]

That is: "when its heat calms." It has been related from Qays that she said: "sakarat al-rih taskuru sukuran," meaning: "it calmed." Even if that is correct from her, the meaning of "sukirat" and "sukkirat," with lightness and doubling, is close; however, the reading that I do not permit anything other than in the Qur'an is ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ with doubling, due to the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it, and it is not permissible to oppose what they have agreed upon.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 15, verse 16:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have placed in the sky great stars, and We have adorned it for the observers﴾ (15:16)

His saying, exalted is He, means: And We placed in the lowest heaven mansions (manazil) for the sun and the moon, and they are stars that the sun and the moon descend into. ﴿And We adorned it for the observers﴾ means: And We adorned the sky with the stars for whoever looks at them and sees them.

Our interpretation accords with what the people of ta'wil (exegesis) have said on this matter.

And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abdullah related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿And We have placed in the sky burujan﴾ he said: stars.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And We have placed in the sky burujan﴾ and its burooj: its stars.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿burujan﴾ he said: the stars.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ (15:17) ﴿except one who eavesdrops, and is pursued by a clear flaming fire﴾ (15:18)**

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: We guarded the lowest heaven from every accursed devil whom Allah has stoned and cursed. ﴿Except one who eavesdrops﴾ means: but some of the devils do eavesdrop on what is decreed in the heaven, so a flaming meteor pursues him, a clear fire that makes its effect evident on him, either by stupefying and corrupting him, or by burning him.

Some of the grammarians of Basra (nahwiyyun, grammarians) said regarding His words ﴿except one who eavesdrops﴾ that it is an exceptional istithna' (exception that is not part of the preceding group), like the saying: "ma ashtaki illa khayran" (I do not complain except of good), meaning: "but I mention good." Some of them denied this view and said: "When illa (except) has the meaning of lakin (but), it takes the governing effect of lakin, and there is no need to supply an implied 'adhkuru' (I mention). If the matter required supplying 'adhkuru' in this way, then the statement of the speaker, 'Zayd stood up, not 'Amr' (qama Zayd la 'Amr), would require supplying 'adhkuru' as well."

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) said in agreement with what we have said.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the earth — We spread it out and cast therein firmly set mountains, and caused to grow therein of every thing in measured proportion (19)﴾

Exalted is He, by His saying ﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾, means: and the earth, We spread it out and laid it flat. ﴿And cast therein firmly set mountains﴾ means: and We cast upon its surfaces firmly set mountains, meaning stable mountains.

As related by:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾. In another verse He said ﴿And after that He spread it out (dahaha)﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:30]. It has been mentioned to us that Umm al-Qura (the mother of cities) is Makkah, and from it the earth was spread out. As for His saying ﴿And caused to grow therein of every thing in measured proportion﴾:

He means: and We caused to grow in the earth of every thing; that is, of every thing determined and within a known limit.

The first of the two opinions is, in our view, the more correct, due to the consensus of the authoritative scholars of interpretation upon it.

The exegesis of the words of the Most High: ﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood, and [also for those] for whom you are not providers﴾ (20)

The Most High says: ﴿And We made for you﴾, O people, on the earth ﴿means of livelihood﴾, which is the plural of *ma'ishah* (livelihood), ﴿and [also for those] for whom you are not providers﴾.

The people of *ta'wil* (interpretation of the Qur'an) differed concerning the meaning of His words ﴿and [also for those] for whom you are not providers﴾. Some said: it refers to beasts and livestock.

Those who said this:

* Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us. And al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us. And al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, he said: Shababa narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us. And al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, he said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih. And al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Ishaq narrated to us, he said: Abdullah, all of them, narrated to us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and [also for those] for whom you are not providers﴾ — beasts and livestock.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of this.

Others said: it refers exclusively to wild animals.

Those who said this:

* Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, he said: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Mansur [[Mansur, whom Shu'ba ibn al-Hajjaj narrates from, is Mansur ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Tamimi al-Ghadani (with a dammah on the ghayn), who narrates from al-Sha'bi, and from whom Shu'ba and Ibn Ulayya narrate. Ibn Ma'in, Ahmad and Abu Dawud declared him trustworthy. Abu Hatim said: "He is not strong; his hadith is written down but not used as evidence." al-Nasa'i said: "He is not strong." In the statement of al-Farra' that we quote beneath the testimony "Hallā saalta" there is a reference to his narration there, in his words "and it has come that they are the wild animals ..." etc. (See the summary of al-Khazraji.)]] concerning this verse: ﴿and [also for those] for whom you are not providers﴾, he said: the wild animals. Thus the interpretation of "man" (who/those) in ﴿and [also for those] for whom you are not providers﴾ according to this interpretation means "mā" (what), and that is rare in the speech of the Arabs.

The most correct view, and the best to say, is that by His words ﴿and [also for those] for whom you are not providers﴾ is meant: slaves, male and female, and beasts and livestock. The meaning then is: "And We made for you therein means of livelihood, and [We made for you] the slaves, the female slaves, the beasts and the livestock." When this is so, it is proper to place "man" in the position of slaves, female slaves and beasts, because the Arabs do this when they wish to speak of beasts together with human beings. This interpretation, which we have stated and to which we have turned the meaning of the speech, holds when "man" is in the accusative position, coordinated (*'atf*, conjoined) with *ma'ayish* (means of livelihood), meaning: "We made for you therein means of livelihood, and We made for you therein those for whom you are not providers."

It has also been said that "man" is in the genitive position (*khafd*), coordinated with the *kaf* and *mim* in His words ﴿And We made for you﴾, meaning: "And We made for you therein means of livelihood and [for] those for whom you are not providers." I think that Mansur, in his statement "it is the wild animals," intended this meaning and meant it. Although this has a basis in Arabic speech, it is rare and weak, because they hardly ever bring a coordinated noun in the genitive case to agree with a pronoun in this way. It occurs at most in the poetry of some of them in cases of necessity, as one of them said:

*Hallā saalta bi-dhī al-jamājim ʿanhumu / wa-abī Nuʿaymin dhī al-liwāʾi al-mukhraqi*
"Why did you not ask about those of Dhu al-Jamajim, and about Abi Nu'aym, the owner of the torn banner?"

[[This verse is among the evidences cited by al-Farra' in his *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* (p. 167 of the University photocopy). He said: "His words 'And We made for you therein means of livelihood' mean the earth. 'And [also for those] for whom you are not providers': 'man' is in the accusative position; the meaning is 'We made for you therein means of livelihood, and [for] the slaves and the female slaves.' It has come down that they are the wild animals and beasts, but 'man' is not used exclusively for beasts, nor for anything other than people. If it is as narrated, we think it right to include the owned ones (*al-mamalik*) among them, on the ground that We have given you dominion over the slaves, the camels, the sheep and the like, as a metaphor. It may also be said that 'man' is in the genitive position, meaning 'We made for you therein means of livelihood and for [those who are] for...' How rarely do the Arabs return to a genitive noun that has been referred to by a pronoun!" And a poet said: "We hang our swords like the wari-tree, / and between them and the ankle is a wide sandy tract." Here he returned "the ankle" (*al-ka'b*) upon "between them" (*baynahā*). And another said: "Why did you not ask..." (the verse above), where he returned "Abi Nu'aym" upon the *ha'* in *ʿanhum*.

I say: this is the passage that al-Farra' pointed to, namely the coordination of a genitive noun upon a pronoun, as in the Most High's words ﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ in Surat al-Nisa'.]]

So he returned "Abi Nu'aym" upon the *ha'* and *mim* in *ʿanhum*, and I have already shown how unsound this is in their speech.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 15, verse 21:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ (15:21).

His saying, exalted is He, means: There is no rain of any kind but that with Us are its depositories, and We send it down only in a measure known to Us for each land, its limit and its extent.

Those who interpret the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said so:

* Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad informed us, from a man, from Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: "No land receives more rain than another land, but Allah apportions it in the land," then he recited ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Juhayfah, from Abdullah, who said: "No year is rainier than another year, but Allah turns it away from whom He wills," then he said ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾.

* al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Mahdi al-Massisi narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Mushir narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Juhayfah, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "No year is rainier than another year, but Allah distributes it wherever He wills, a year here and a year there," then he recited ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, regarding ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories﴾: "It refers specifically to rain."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Salim informed us, from al-Hakam ibn Utaybah, concerning His saying ﴿and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾, who said: "No year has more rain than another, or less, but rain falls on one people and is withheld from others, and perhaps it falls in the sea." He said: "It has reached us that with the rain there descend angels more in number than the offspring of Iblis and the offspring of Adam, who count every drop, where it falls and what it causes to grow."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 15, verse 22:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing, then We sent down water from the sky and gave you drink from it, and you are not its storers.﴾

The readers differed in their recitation of this. The majority of readers recited ﴿وَأَرْسَلْنَا الرِّيَاحَ لَوَاقِحَ﴾ ("And We sent the winds fertilizing"), while some readers of Kufa recited "وأرْسَلْنا الرّيحَ لَوَاقِحَ" ("And We sent the wind fertilizing"), using the singular "wind" while describing it with the plural "fertilizing" (lawaqih). The meaning of this should be that although the word "wind" is singular, its meaning is plural, because it is said: "The wind came from every direction" and "it blew from every place," so it is described as "fertilizing" on that account. Its plural adjective therefore refers to its meaning, although its wording is singular, in the same way as the Arabs say: "arḍ sabāsib" (a wide land), "arḍ aghfāl" (a land without landmarks), and "thawb akhlāq" (a worn garment), as the poet said:

The winter has come, and my shirt is worn out,
Tattered, at which the one who sews laughs.

[[This verse was cited by al-Farra in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (p. 167). He said: "His statement 'and We sent the winds fertilizing' — and it is recited 'al-rih', as Hamza recited. Whoever says 'al-rih lawaqih' pluralizes the adjective while the noun is singular, because al-rih carries the sense of a plural. Do you not see that you say: 'the wind came from every place,' so it is described as 'lawaqih' on that account, just as one says: 'you left him in arḍ aghfāl and sabāsib,' and 'mahāriq,' and 'thawb akhlāq,' and from it the poet's words: 'The winter has come...' the verse. As for whoever says 'al-riyāh lawaqih,' it is clear; but it is said: the wind is fertilizing (mulqiha), it fertilizes the trees, so how is it said 'lawaqih'? In that there are two meanings: one is that the wind is what, by its passing over the dust and water, has in it fertilization, so it is said 'rih laqih,' as one says 'nāqa laqih' (a pregnant she-camel). A witness to this is that He described the wind of punishment, saying 'upon them the sterile wind,' making it sterile since it did not fertilize. The other way is that it is described as 'laqih' even though it fertilizes, as one says 'a sleeping night' while sleep is in it, and 'a concealed secret.' And in Lisan al-Arab (khalaqa): it is said 'thawb akhlāq,' they describe the single item with it when the worn-out state is in all of it, as the one who said 'burma a'shār' (a pot of tens) and 'thawb akbāsh' (a type of Yemeni weave) and 'ḥabl armām' and 'arḍ sabāsib,' and such usage is abundant; likewise 'mulā'a akhlāq' and 'burma akhlāq' (from al-Liḥyani), meaning its sides are worn. He said: it is from the singular which was divided and then pluralized. He said: likewise 'ḥabl akhlāq' and 'qirba akhlāf' from Ibn al-A'rabi. Al-Tahdhib: it is said 'thawb akhlāq' gathering what is around it. The rajiz said: 'The winter has come...' the verse. And al-Tawwaq is his son. I say: the narration in al-Farra and in Lisan is 'yaḍḥaku minhu,' and with the author 'yaḍḥaku minnī,' and the meaning is close to one another.]]

And so the Arabs do with everything that is broad.

The people of Arabic grammar differed on the reason for describing the winds as "laqiḥ" (fertilized/fertilizing), since they are actually "mulqiha" (causing fertilization), not "laqiha" — because they fertilize the clouds and the trees. Describing something as "laqiḥ" properly applies to what is fertilized, not the fertilizer, as one says "nāqa laqiḥ" (a pregnant she-camel). Some grammarians of Basra said: it is said "al-riyāḥ lawāqiḥ," and they made it on the pattern of "laqiḥ," as if the winds had become pregnant, because in them there is good, so they have become pregnant with good. He said: some of them said: "The winds fertilize the clouds," and this indicates that meaning, because when they produce it and there is good in them, that good reaches it. Some grammarians of Kufa said: in that there are two meanings: one is that the wind is what fertilizes by its passing over the dust and water, so there is fertilization in it, and it is said "rīḥ laqiḥ," as one says "nāqa laqiḥ." He said: a witness to this is that He described the wind of punishment, saying ﴿upon them the sterile wind﴾, making it sterile when it did not fertilize. He said: The other way is that it is described as "laqiḥ" even though it fertilizes, as one says "a sleeping night" while sleep is in it, and "a concealed secret," and as one says "al-mabrūz" and "al-makhtūm" — so "mabrūz" (brought out) is used rather than "mubrez," built on other than its verb, meaning that this is one of its attributes, so an object form may be used in place of an active form, just as an active form may be used in place of an object form, when one does not intend to build on the verb, as one says "mā' dāfiq" (gushing water).

The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that the winds are "lawāqiḥ" as He, may His praise be exalted, described them, and though they fertilize the clouds and the trees, they are both "lāqiḥa" and "mulqiḥa." Their fertilization (luqḥ) is their carrying of water, and their causing fertilization of the clouds and trees (ilqāḥ) is their working in it. This is as 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said:

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Muharibi narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal ibn 'Amr, from Qays ibn Sakan, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding His statement ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾: He said: Allah sends the winds, and they carry the water, and they set the clouds in motion, so they give milk as a she-camel gives milk, then it rains.

⁕ Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Qays ibn Sakan, from 'Abdullah: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾: He said: Allah sends the wind, and it fertilizes the clouds, then it stirs them so they give milk as a she-camel gives milk, then it rains.

⁕ al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal ibn 'Amr, from Qays ibn al-Sakan, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding His statement ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾: He said: He sends the winds, and they carry the water from the clouds, then they stir the clouds, so they give milk as a she-camel gives milk. So 'Abdullah made clear by his statement, "He sends the winds, and they carry the water," that they are the ones that fertilize by carrying the water, even though they are also fertilizing by fertilizing the clouds and the trees.

As for other groups among the interpreters, they took God's description of them as "lawāqiḥ" to mean "mulqiḥa" (causing fertilization), and that "lawāqiḥ" was placed in the position of "mulāqiḥ," as Nahshal ibn Hari said:

Let Yazid weep, the wretched one for his affliction,
And the disheveled one whom the calamities have tossed.

[[The verse is by Nahshal ibn Hari according to the most correct view, a Mukhadram poet, though it is sometimes attributed to others; al-Baghdadi preferred its attribution to Nahshal. Abu 'Ubayda cited it in this same version when interpreting His statement "And We sent the winds fertilizing," saying: its figurative usage is that of "mulāqiḥ," because the wind fertilizes the clouds, as the Arabs do. He does this, omitting the "m," because it returns it to the original of the speech, as the saying of Nahshal ibn Hari lamenting his brother: "Liabki Yazid..." the verse. He dropped the "m," because it is the passive form. The author of Lisan (ṭayḥ) cited the verse with variation in some words, and said: Sibawayh recited: "Let Yazid weep, one who is hurt by a dispute, and one who is beaten by what the calamities strike." Sibawayh said: "al-ṭawā'iḥ" is on the omission of the extra letter, or on the nisba. Ibn Jinni said: the beginning of the verse is built on dropping that agent, for its end (as in Lisan) has returned the speech to the agent, since its implied meaning afterwards is: "Let the one beaten by what the calamities strike weep," so his words "liyabki" (passive) indicate what he meant by "liyabki" (active). And al-mukhtabit is one who travels in whatever direction without knowledge or means. See Khizanat al-Adab by al-Baghdadi (1: 147–152), where there is much discussion of the meaning, transmission and speaker of the verse.]] meaning "mutāliḥ" (the ones who are made to fertilize), and as al-Nabigha said:

Leave me to a concern, O Umayma, that wearies,
And a night I endure, slow of stars.

[[The verse is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, the opening of an ode praising 'Amr ibn al-Harith al-A'raj, son of al-Harith al-Akbar, son of Abi Shamir, when he fled from al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir. We have explained it elsewhere in this tafsir. The witness here is his word "nāṣib" (wearying), that it means "munṣib" (causing weariness). In Lisan (nasaba): al-nasab is fatigue from toil. The verb: nasiba al-rajul (with kasra) — he became tired and exhausted; and anṣabahu he (caused it), and anṣabanī this matter, and "hum nāṣib" (they are wearied): "munṣib," possessing weariness, like "tāmir" and "labin," and it is an active participle in the sense of a passive one, because he is wearied in it and tired. Al-Nabigha said: "Leave me to a concern..." He said: "nāṣib" means "manṣūb" (afflicted), and al-Asma'i said: "nāṣib" means "dhū naṣab" (one possessing weariness), like "laylun nā'im" (a sleeping night) possessing sleep in it, and "rajul dāri'" (a man wearing armour) possessing armour. Sibawayh said: "hum nāṣib" is on the nisba (relational form), and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi recorded its being "nāṣib" to them, so "nāṣib" is then on the verb. I say: Does Abu 'Ali al-Farisi mean that it is a regular active participle following its verb, so it is not on the nisba, nor on the figurative attribution like "laylun nā'im"?]]

in the sense of "munṣib" (causing weariness).

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, regarding His statement ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾: He said: It fertilizes the clouds.

⁕ al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, the like of it.

⁕ Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, the like of it.

⁕ Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His statement ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾: He said: fertilizing for the trees. I said: or for the clouds? He said: and for the clouds, stirring them until it rains.

⁕ al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: Allah sends the bearers of good news (al-mubashshirat), and they spread the earth out flat; then Allah sends the stirrers (al-muthirat), and they stir the clouds; then Allah sends the gatherers (al-mu'allifat), and they gather the clouds; then Allah sends the fertilizers (al-lawaqih), and they fertilize the trees. Then 'Ubayd recited ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾.

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His statement ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾: He says: fertilizing the clouds; and among the wind is punishment, and among it is mercy.

⁕ Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, ﴿fertilizing﴾: He said: it fertilizes the water in the clouds.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿fertilizing﴾: He said: it fertilizes the trees and sets the clouds in motion.

⁕ I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His statement ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾: The winds Allah sends over the clouds, and they fertilize them, so they become full of water.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Yunus narrated to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Maymun narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Mahzam narrated to us, from Abu Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The south wind is from Paradise, and it is the fertilizing wind (al-rih al-lawaqih), and it is the one Allah mentioned in His Book, and in it are benefits for people."

⁕ Abu al-Jamahir al-Himsi or al-Hadrami Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Maymun Abu 'Ubayda narrated to us, from Abu al-Mahzam, from Abu Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he mentioned the like of it exactly.

* *

As for His statement ﴿And We sent down water from the sky and gave you drink from it﴾:

He, the Exalted, says: We sent down rain from the sky and gave you drink from that rain, for the watering of your land and your livestock. Had the meaning been "We sent it down so that you might drink it," it would have been said "fa-saqaynākumūhu" without the alif. That is because when the Arabs give a man water to drink, or milk or other things, they say "saqaytuhu" without the alif if it is for his drinking; but if they provide water for his land or his livestock to drink, they say "asqaytuhu," "asqaytu arḍahu" and "asqaytu māshiyatahu." Likewise, if they ask for water on his behalf, they say "asqaytuhu" and "istasqaytuhu," as Dhu al-Rummah said:

I stopped at the traces of Maya's dwelling, my she-camel,
So I kept weeping there and addressing it...
And I give it to drink (asqihi) until its stones and its playgrounds
Almost speak to me of what I complain of to it.

[[These two verses are in the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah (Cambridge edition, 1919, p. 38). "Asqīhi": I invoke for it the blessing of rain, I say: may God water you. "Abuththuhu": I complain to it. Abu 'Ubayda cited these two verses in Majaz al-Qur'an (1: 350) as evidence that one says "saqaytu al-rajul mā'an wa sharāban min laban wa ghayr dhālika" (I gave a man water and drink of milk and other things), and there is only one dialect in it, without alif, when it is for drinking; and when you make drink for him (shirb, with kasra on the shin, meaning water for his animals to drink), it is "asqaytuhu," "asqaytu arḍahu" and "ibilahu," and it cannot be otherwise; likewise if you ask for water on his behalf, as in Dhu al-Rummah's saying... the two verses, which is close to the author's statement here.]]

Likewise, if you gave a man a hide so that he would make it a water-skin, you would say "asqaytuhu iyyāhu" (I gave him water with it).

* *

As for His statement ﴿and you are not its storers﴾:

He says: You are not storers of the water which We sent down from the sky and gave you to drink, so that you could withhold it from drinking. That is because it is in My hand and under My control: I give it to drink to whom I will, and I withhold it from whom I will.

As it was narrated:

⁕ Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying Sufyan: ﴿and you are not its storers﴾ — he said: withholders.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 15, verse 23–25:

The interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritors (of the earth and all upon it).﴾ (23) ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ (24) ﴿And indeed, your Lord – it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise and Knowing.﴾ (25)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿And indeed, it is We who give life﴾ to whoever was dead, when We wish, ﴿and cause death﴾ to whoever was alive, when We will, ﴿and We are the Inheritors﴾ – meaning: We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, by causing all of them to die, so that no living being remains besides Us when that appointed term comes.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding its interpretation. Some of them said: The meaning of that is: We have known those of the nations who passed away, whose destruction came earlier, and those who have been created and are alive, and those who have not yet been created but will be created.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from his father, from Ikrimah: ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ He said: The preceding ones: those who have been created and those of the nations who passed away; and the later ones: those who have not been created.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Qays narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Masruq, from Ikrimah, regarding His saying ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ He said: They are all of God's creation; He has known those of them who were created up to today, and He has known those who He will create after today.

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn al-Taymi informed us, from his father, from Ikrimah, who said: God created the creation and then finished with them. So the preceding ones are those who have come out of the creation, and the later ones are those who remain in the loins of men and have not come out.

- Muhammad ibn Abi Ma'shar narrated to me, saying: Abu Ma'shar informed me, saying: I heard 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud discussing with Muhammad ibn Ka'b concerning the saying of God ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud said: The best of the rows of men is the front, and the worst of the rows of men is the back; and the best of the rows of women is the back, and the worst of the rows of women is the front. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: It is not so. Rather: ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you﴾ are the dead and the slain, and the later ones are those who will follow them after; ﴿And indeed, your Lord – it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise and Knowing.﴾ 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah said: May God grant you success and reward you with good.

- Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, from his father, who said: Qatadah said: The preceding ones: those who have passed away; and the later ones: those who remain in the loins of men.

- al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Masruq narrated to us, from Ikrimah and Khusayf, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ The two said: Those who died and those who remain.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you﴾ He said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say: Adam (ﷺ) and whoever passed away of his offspring. ﴿And We have known the later ones﴾: those who remain in the loins of men.

- Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ He said: The preceding ones are Adam and those after him, until this verse was revealed; and the later ones: He said: everyone who was of his offspring.

Abu Ja'far said: I think that I said: what has not been created and what is created.

- Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from his father, from Ikrimah, who said: The preceding ones: what has come out of the loins of men; and the later ones: what has not come out. Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, your Lord – it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise and Knowing.﴾

And others said: By the preceding ones is meant those who have perished, and by the later ones are meant the living who have not perished.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ He meant by the preceding ones: those who died, and by the later ones: those who are alive and have not died.

- I was told on the authority of al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His saying ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you﴾: meaning the dead among you; ﴿And We have already known the later ones﴾: their remnant, who are the living. He says: We have known those who died and those who remain.

- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ He said: The preceding ones among you: those who passed away at the beginning of the nations; and the later ones: those who remain.

And others said: Rather, its meaning is: We have known the preceding ones at the beginning of creation and the later ones at its end.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from 'Amir, regarding this verse ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ He said: the first of creation and its last.

And others said: Rather, its meaning is: We have known the preceding ones among you in goodness, and those who lag behind from it.

And others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: We have known the preceding ones among you in the rows during prayer, and those who lag behind in it because of women.

Mention of those who said that:

He said: So God revealed ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: 'Amr ibn Malik informed me, saying: I heard Abu al-Jawza' say regarding the saying of God ﴿And We have already known the preceding ones among you, and We have known the later ones.﴾ He said: The preceding ones among you in the rows during prayer, and the later ones.

- Muhammad ibn Musa al-Harashi narrated to me, saying: Nuh ibn Qays narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Malik narrated to us, from Abu al-Jawza', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A woman used to pray behind the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas said: No, by God, I have never seen anyone like her. The people of interpretation said the like of what we have said regarding this.
